title: Gateway Patterns for Tool Loading
tierLabel: Infrastructure -- a service you stand up
summary: Progressive disclosure (Tab 5) solved this for one agent with a fixed tool list. At scale -- dozens of MCP servers, hundreds of tools across a fleet of agents -- static loading is itself the bottleneck, and you need a gateway that resolves and loads tool definitions on demand.
whyItMatters: Connecting an agent to many MCP servers directly means loading every server's full tool catalog on every call, even though a given task might use tools from only one or two of them. A gateway centralizes discovery so agents load only what they need, when they need it.

concepts.heading: The gateway sits between the agent and many tool sources
concepts.body: Rather than an agent connecting directly to N MCP servers and receiving all N catalogs, it connects to one gateway. The gateway indexes every downstream server's tools and exposes a search/discovery interface -- the agent asks 'what tools handle X' and gets back only relevant results, not everything.

concepts.heading: Tool search as a first-class capability, not an afterthought
concepts.body: A gateway's core value is a search tool over tool metadata: given a natural-language description of what's needed, return the matching tool(s) and only then load their full schema into context. This is the fleet-scale version of the single-agent progressive disclosure in Tab 5.

concepts.heading: Centralized auth, policy, and rate limiting
concepts.body: A gateway is also the natural place to enforce which agents can reach which downstream tools, apply rate limits per tool/server, and centralize credential management -- so individual agents don't each need their own connection and auth logic to every MCP server, which would multiply both complexity and standing connection overhead.

exercises.title: Stand up a minimal tool-search gateway over two mock MCP-style tool sources
exercises.goal: Demonstrate the discovery-then-load pattern end-to-end: an agent asks a gateway for relevant tools by description, gets back a short list, and only then requests full schemas for the ones it needs.
steps: Define two mock 'downstream servers,' each with 3-4 tools and a one-line description per tool (simulating two MCP servers with disjoint catalogs).

Build a gateway search function that takes a free-text query and returns the top-matching tool names + descriptions across both servers (simple keyword match is enough to demonstrate the pattern; a real gateway would use embeddings).
Give the agent only the gateway's `search_tools(query)` and `get_tool_schema(name)` meta-tools -- not the full catalogs of either downstream server.

Run a task that only needs one server's tools. → Expect: search_tools returns matches from the relevant server only; get_tool_schema is called only for the 1-2 tools actually used; the other server's tool definitions never enter context at all.
exercises.costImpact: Without a gateway, connecting to both servers directly means loading 6+ full tool schemas (both servers) on every call regardless of task. With gateway-mediated search, only the 1-2 relevant schemas for the matched server are loaded -- the unused server's entire catalog costs zero tokens for that task.
